title: Soil formation and why topsoil is irreplaceable
text:
Soil is not crushed rock, and the distinction is the whole of today's lecture. Crushed rock is a starting material. Soil is what happens when that material is worked on for a very long time by water, by climate and above all by living things.

The sequence runs something like this. Rock is broken down physically, by frost and by heat, and chemically, by slightly acidic rainwater dissolving its minerals. Pioneer organisms colonise the debris. When they die, their remains are decomposed by fungi and bacteria into humus, a dark organic material that holds water, stores nutrients and binds mineral particles into crumbs. Those crumbs are what give a good soil its structure, letting air and roots penetrate while resisting erosion. Over centuries this produces distinct horizontal layers, or horizons: organic matter at the surface, a leached layer beneath it where percolating water has carried minerals downwards, and an accumulation layer where those minerals are deposited. Climate, parent rock, slope, organisms and time together determine the result, which is why soils differ so sharply between regions. The practical consequence is sobering. A centimetre of topsoil may take a century or more to develop, and a single season of bad management can remove it.
points: Soil is not merely crushed rock; it is rock material transformed over long periods by water, climate and living organisms.
Rock is broken down physically by frost and heat and chemically by slightly acidic rainwater.
Dead organisms are decomposed into humus, which holds water and nutrients and binds particles into crumbs, giving the soil its structure and resisting erosion.
Over centuries the soil develops distinct layers or horizons: organic matter on top, a leached layer below, and a layer where the washed-down minerals accumulate.
Climate, parent rock, slope, organisms and time together explain why soils differ between regions.
Topsoil forms extremely slowly, perhaps a centimetre per century, but can be lost in a single season.
